'''Tarjumo''', also known as '''Old Kanembu''' or '''Classical Kanembu''', is a [[Classical language|classical]] and [[sacred language]] created and used by [[Muslim scholars]] in the [[Kanem–Bornu Empire]], located in the central [[Sahel]]. It likely emerged in the 15th century as a liturgical and scholarly language for [[tafsir|Qur'anic exegesis]] and grammatical analysis of sacred texts in [[Classical Arabic|classical arabic]]. The name Tarjumo derives from the [[Arabic]] verb ''tarjama'' (ترجم), meaning "to translate."

It is classified within the [[Nilo-Saharan languages|Nilo-Saharan language family]],<ref>{{Cite web |title=Glottolog 5.1 - Tarjumo |url=https://glottolog.org/resource/languoid/id/tarj1235 |access-date=2025-04-02 |website=glottolog.org}}</ref> although this classification is debated among linguists.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Errington |first=Joseph |date=2001 |title=Colonial Linguistics |url=https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev.anthro.30.1.19 |journal=Annual Review of Anthropology |language=en |volume=30 |issue=1 |pages=30–34 |doi=10.1146/annurev.anthro.30.1.19 |issn=0084-6570|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Demoule |first=Jean-Paul |url=https://www.worldcat.org/title/894848931 |title=Mais où sont passés les Indo-Européens? le mythe d'origine de l'Occident |date=2014 |publisher=Éditions du Seuil |isbn=978-2-02-029691-5 |series=La librairie du XXIe siècle |location=Paris |oclc=894848931}}</ref> Old Kanembu is an early form of the Kanuri language, which became fixed through its liturgical use before the dialectal split that led to the emergence of Kanembu, spoken in the northeast of [[Lake Chad]] in present-day [[Chad]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |url=https://www.degruyter.com/document/doi/10.1515/9781614510543/html |title=Scribes as Agents of Language Change |date=2013|publisher=De Gruyter   |isbn=978-1-61451-050-5 |editor-last=Wagner |editor-first=Esther-Miriam |chapter=Language change induced by written codes: a case of Old Kanembu and Kanuri dialects |doi=10.1515/9781614510543 |editor-last2=Outhwaite |editor-first2=Ben |editor-last3=Beinhoff |editor-first3=Bettina}}</ref> As a result, it retains linguistic features shared with the [[Teda language|Teda]]-[[Daza language|Daza]] and [[Beria language|Beria]] languages.<ref name=":0" /> The Tarjumo language uses the Arabic script, and represents a complementary practice to Ajami in vernacular languages. Scholars primarily used it for grammatical analysis and the Qur’anic exegesis of sacred texts in [[Classical Arabic]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bondarev |first=Dmitry |date=2013 |title=Qur'anic Exegesis in Old Kanembu: Linguistic Precision for Better Interpretation |url=https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/jqs.2013.0114 |journal=Journal of Qur'anic Studies |language=en |volume=15 |issue=3 |pages=56–83 |doi=10.3366/jqs.2013.0114 |issn=1465-3591|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Today, Tarjumo is still used in glossing and Qur'anic exegesis ([[Tafsir]]) by a limited circle of Muslim scholars in [[Borno State]], [[Nigeria]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Tamari |first=Tal |last2=Bondarev |first2=Dmitry |date=2013 |title=Introduction and Annotated Bibliography |url=https://www.euppublishing.com/doi/10.3366/jqs.2013.0113 |journal=Journal of Qur'anic Studies |language=en |volume=15 |issue=3 |pages=1–55 |doi=10.3366/jqs.2013.0113 |issn=1465-3591|url-access=subscription }}</ref> as well as in southeastern [[Niger]], particularly in [[Zinder]] and Kribitoa, in the [[Diffa Region|Diffa]] Region.<ref name=":5">{{Cite web |last=Awagana |first=Ari |title=Old kanembu Project |url=https://langarchiv.hypotheses.org/old-kanembu-project |access-date=2025-04-02 |website=Langarchiv |language=fr-FR}}</ref> [[File:Coran de Chétima de Zinder.jpg|thumb|Manuscript fragment of a Qur'an with annotations in Old Kanembu, displaying interlinear and marginal commentary. The manuscript belongs to the Chétima family archives in Zinder. Photograph by Ari Awagana, ERC Langarchiv project.|alt=Photograph of an Ancient fragment of a Quran manuscript annotated in Old Kanembu, featuring circular decorative motifs. The document features several circular decorative motifs in brown and yellow along the margins, as well as detailed handwritten commentary in Old Kanembu, inserted interlinearly and in the margins. The parchment shows visible signs of wear and old repairs, with thread stitching running through the paper.|449x449px]]

== History ==

=== Emergence (12th–15th Centuries) ===
The Tarjumo language is a part of the African literacy associated with Islamic scholarship in the Sahara-Sahel region, referred to as the "African Library" by [[Ousmane Oumar Kane|Ousmane Omar Kane]].<ref name=Kane2016>{{Cite book |last=Kane |first=Ousmane |title=Beyond Timbuktu: An Intellectual History of Muslim West Africa |date=2016 |publisher=Harvard University Press |isbn=978-0-674-96937-7 |location=Cambridge, MA}}</ref>{{rp|34}}  Kanem was one of the earliest regions in the Sahara and Sahel to embrace Islam, with evidence of Islamic scholarly culture dating back to the 12th century during the reign of the [[Sayfawa dynasty|Sayfawa]] dynasty.<ref name=Kane2016/>{{rp|34}}<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Imam |first=Yahya Oyewole |date=2004 |title=The Tradition of Qur'anic Learning in Borno / ‮يحيي اوياولي ٳمام، دراسة القرآن في بورنو‬ |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/25728152 |journal=Journal of Qur'anic Studies |volume=6 |issue=2 |pages=96–102 |issn=1465-3591|jstor=25728152}}</ref> In the 13th century, the writings of the Kanem poet and scholar al-Kanemi were noted by the Arab biographer [[Ibn Khallikan]].<ref name=Kane2016/>{{rp|43}} Islamic scholars and experts in Quranic sciences received financial support from the Kanem court, along with numerous privileges granted through charters known as ''mahrams''.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bobboyi |first=Hamidu |date=1993 |title=Relations of the Borno ʿulamāʾ with the Sayfawa Rulers: The Role of the Maḥrams |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/25653229 |journal=Sudanic Africa |volume=4 |pages=175–204 |issn=0803-0685|jstor=25653229}}</ref>

=== Written tradition in Old Kanembu ===
[[File:Kanem-Bornu 1650.svg|thumb|Map showing the extent of the Kanem–Bornu Empire's territories in the 18th century|alt= Historical map showing in green the territorial extent of the Kanem–Bornu Empire in the 18th century, covering areas around Lake Chad, including parts of present-day Nigeria, Niger, Chad, and Cameroon.|477x477px]]
It is within this favorable context for the production and transmission of Islamic scholarly knowledge that the practice of Quranic glossing in what is now referred to as Old Kanembu is believed to have emerged. The oldest known Old Kanembu manuscripts, such as the Geidam Quran, date back to the 17th century, they attest to an exegetical tradition that predates them.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bondarev |first=Dimitri |date=2013 |title=Qur'anic Exegesis in Old Kanembu: Linguistic Precision for Better Interpretation / تفسير القرآن باالكانيمبو القديمة: الدقة اللغوية لتفسير أفضل |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/24283579 |journal=Journal of Qur'anic Studies |volume=15 |issue=3 |page=57 |quote=The antiquity of the Bomo tafslr tradition is further supported by the analysis of the linguistic structures of Old Kanembu as evidenced in the language of Qur'an glosses; these point to earlier periods in the development of the Kanembu and Kanuri languages. |jstor=24283579}}</ref>

In the 16th century, when the [[Sayfawa dynasty]] moved from Kanem to Bornu, southeast of [[Lake Chad]], these scholarly practices spread to the new regions. In the 18th century, the Bornu Sultanate played a central role in [[trans-Saharan trade]] between [[Kano (city)|Kano]] and [[Tripoli, Libya|Tripoli]], utilizing the route through [[Bilma]], the [[Kaouar]] oases, and [[Fezzan]]. Kanuri served as the [[lingua franca]] along this route, while written culture in Arabic, Kanuri Ajami, and Old Kanembu flourished.<ref name=":3">{{Cite book |last=Lefebvre |first=Camille |url=https://www.worldcat.org/title/on1253469157 |title=Des pays au crépuscule: le moment de l'occupation coloniale (Sahara-Sahel) |date=2021 |publisher=Fayard |isbn=978-2-213-71810-1 |series=Collection "L'épreuve de l'histoire" |location=Paris |oclc=on1253469157}}</ref>[[File:Fourth-page-of-the-Geidam-Quran-manuscript-1YM-containing-ayats-20-to-25-of-the.png|thumb|Photograph by A.D.H. Bivar (late 1950s) showing a page of the 'Geidam Quran' (manuscript 1YM). This fourth page contains verses 20 to 25 of Surah Al-Baqara, annotated with interlinear commentary in Old Kanembu.|alt=Black-and-white image showing an ancient manuscript page of the Quran, featuring dense interlinear and marginal annotations in Old Kanembu script. |471x471px]]

=== Marginalization ===
At the turn of the 20th century, part of the intellectual elite of Bornu went into exile, including figures such as Al-Hajj Musa ibn Hissein,<ref>{{Cite book |url=https://brill.com/edcollbook/title/71841 |title=L'œuvre en kanouri d'al-Hajj Musa ibn Hissein, un savant du Borno (Niger-Nigéria) |year=2025 |publisher=Brill |isbn=978-90-04-72403-7 |editor-last=Awagana |editor-first=Ari |language=fr |editor-last2=Lefebvre |editor-first2=Camille}}</ref> following the conquest of the Bornu Sultanate by the warlord [[Rabih az-Zubayr|Rabih]], and subsequent [[Colonialism|colonial occupations]] by the [[French colonial empire|French]], [[British Empire|British]], and [[German colonial empire|Germans]] in the region.<ref name=":3" /><ref>{{Cite book |last=Hiribarren |first=Vincent |title=A history of Borno: Trans-Saharan African empire to failing Nigerian state |date=2017 |publisher=Hurst & Company |isbn=978-1-84904-474-5 |location=London}}</ref> Colonial rule led to the marginalization in Western scholarship of West African Arabic and Ajami literary cultures.<ref name=Kane2016/><nowiki>|rp|21–41}} However, Ajami manuscripts from the Central Sahara-Sahel were already known to certain </nowiki>[[Anglicanism|Anglican]] missionaries of the [[Church Missionary Society]] by the late 19th century.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Philips |first=John Edward |title=Spurious Arabic: Hausa and colonial Nigeria |date=2000 |publisher=African Studies Program, University of Wisconsin |isbn=978-0-942615-45-6 |location=Madison, WI}}</ref>

These scholarly and literary traditions from the Sahel and Central Sahara were rediscovered in the late 1950s and 1960s by British academics based in Nigeria, such as W.E.N. Kensdale and [[John Hunwick]] from the [[University of Ibadan]], and [[A.D.H. Bivar]] from the Department of Antiquities in [[Jos]].<ref name=Kane2016/>{{rp|34}} In 1959, Bivar, identified ancient Quran manuscripts—including one dated to 1st Jumādā 1080 AH (26 October 1669)—annotated in Arabic and a previously unknown second language.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Awagana |first=Ari |title=Old kanembu Project |url=https://langarchiv.hypotheses.org/old-kanembu-project |access-date=2025-04-02 |website=Langarchiv |language=en}}</ref>  In the 2000s, Dimitry Bondarev analyzed and identified this language, naming it Old Kanembu.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bondarev |first=Dmitry |date=2006 |title=The language of the glosses in the Bornu quranic manuscripts |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/bulletin-of-the-school-of-oriental-and-african-studies/article/abs/language-of-the-glosses-in-the-bornu-quranic-manuscripts/FE6ED12954FE734DDB3BBB5A39F755AD |journal=Bulletin of SOAS |language=en |volume=69 |issue=1 |pages=113–140 |doi=10.1017/S0041977X06000061 |issn=1474-0699|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

== Old Kanembu as a scriptural language ==

=== Glossing ===
The scholarly communities of Bornu employ Old Kanembu as a specialized medium for the interpretation and transmission of Qur'anic knowledge.<ref>{{Cite book |title=Manuscript cultures: mapping the field |date=2014 |publisher=De Gruyter |isbn=978-3-11-022563-1 |editor-last=Quenzer |editor-first=Jörg B. |series=Studies in manuscript cultures |location=Berlin Boston |pages=113–155 |editor-last2=Bondarev |editor-first2=Dmitry |editor-last3=Sobisch |editor-first3=Jan-Ulrich}}</ref> Annotations and commentaries in Old Kanembu adhered to a codified system. The stability of the practice is evidenced by manuscripts that were annotated successively by multiple scribes.<ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last=Hirji |first=Zulfikar Amir |title=Approaches to the Qur'an in Sub-Saharan Africa |date=2019 |publisher=Oxford University Press The Institute of Ismaili Studies |isbn=978-0-19-884077-0 |series=Qur'anic Studies Series |location=Oxford; New York, NY; London |chapter=2: Tafsīr Sources in Four Annotated Qur'anic Manuscripts from Ancient Borno, Dmitry Bondarev}}</ref> The manuscripts are in [[Loose leaf|loose-leaf]] format, with [[catchword]]s written on the verso to maintain the correct order of folios. The leaves are typically bundled using protective boards, a leather folder, or a custom-made [[satchel]].<ref>{{Citation |last=Bondarev |first=Dmitry |title=Loose-leaf Islamic Manuscripts of West Africa: Retention, Adaptation or Invention? |date=2023 |work=Tied and Bound: A Comparative View on Manuscript Binding |pages=285–300 |url=https://www.degruyterbrill.com:443/document/doi/10.1515/9783111292069-010/html |access-date=2025-04-04 |publisher=De Gruyter |language=en |doi=10.1515/9783111292069-010 |isbn=978-3-11-129206-9|doi-access=free }}</ref>

Depending on the manuscript, annotations appear directly alongside the main text, interlinearly for grammatical or semantic clarification, or in the margins, according to the type of analysis required.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Quenzer |first=Jörg B. |title=Exploring Written Artefacts |date=2021 |publisher=De Gruyter |isbn=978-3-11-075330-1 |series=Studies in Manuscript Cultures |location=Berlin/Boston |pages=711–728}}</ref> These glosses are frequently accompanied by quotations from Classical Arabic exegetical sources.<ref name=":1" /> By combining [[translation]], commentary, and Qur'anic interpretation, the glosses in Old Kanembu illustrate how linguistic code-switching influences the understanding of sacred texts.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Bondarev |first=Dimitri |title=African Literacies : Ideologies, Scripts, Education |publisher=Cambridge Scholars Publishing |year=2014 |isbn=978-1-4438-5833-5 |editor-last=Juffermans |editor-first=Kasper Cornelis Pieter |pages=19 |language=en |chapter=Performance of Multilayered Literacy: Tarjumo of the Kanuri Muslim Scholars |quote=Tarjumo is a Metalanguage Used For Grammatical Analysis of Arabic, with Embedded Interpreting Power  |editor-last2=Asfaha |editor-first2=Yonas Mesfun |editor-last3=Abdelhay |editor-first3=Ashraf}}</ref>

=== Practices blending oral and written traditions ===
One of the distinctive features of scholarly practices and education in the Saharo-Sahelian regions is the interplay between the written Arabic of the sacred text and the African vernacular languages. This blending of modes reflects a continuum between written and [[oral tradition]]s characteristic of Sahelian cultures.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Barber |first=Karin |url=https://www.worldcat.org/title/154706318 |title=The anthropology of texts, persons and publics: oral and written culture in Africa and beyond |date=2007 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-83787-3 |series=New departures in anthropology |location=Cambridge; New York |oclc=154706318}}</ref> Passages of the Qur'an are first recited aloud in Arabic and then orally translated by the scholar into vernacular languages. It is within this intellectual context that Old Kanembu [[exegesis|exegetical practices]] take place, closely tied to oral interpretative [[Performance studies|performance]].{{citation needed|date=April 2025}}

During these performances, the Qur'an is recited from memory by scholars, typically beginning with the shorter final ''[[Surah|sūrahs]].'' Each passage is divided into units of meaning and analyzed with reference to classical exegetical texts (''tafsīr''), such as the [[Tafsir al-Jalalayn|Tafsīr al-Jalālayn]] compiled by [[Al-Suyuti|Jalāl ad-Dīn al-Suyūṭī]] in 1505.{{citation needed|date=April 2025}} These commentaries, generally read from written sources, inform the translation and interpretation of each unit of meaning into Tarjumo. The scholar adapts the format of their recitation to the [[audience]], either condensing or elaborating the commentary depending on the context. In more informal settings, where audience comprehension is essential, recitations are often interspersed with commentary in vernacular Kanuri.{{citation needed|date=April 2025}}

=== Contemporary uses within Bornu Muslim communities ===
Old Kanembu continues to be used today in the Nigerian state of [[Borno State|Borno]], particularly in its capital, [[Maiduguri]], as well as in neighbouring regions of southeastern [[Niger]] such as [[Damagaram]], Manga, and [[Damerghu|Damergou]].<ref name=":5" /> In these areas, a modernized form of the language is sometimes referred to as ''Tarjumo-Kanembu''. It remains highly valued within the Kanuri-speaking community for its religious and cultural significance. Mastery of Old Kanembu is considered prestigious and constitutes a central component of advanced classical Islamic education (''sangaya''). It is publicly employed during [[Qur'anic exegesis]] performances (''tarjumo'') at significant events such as Arabic poetry competitions (''[[Qasida|qasīda]]''), invocations, and recitations held throughout the month of [[Ramadan]].{{Citation needed|date=April 2025}}

== Linguistic features ==

=== Phonology ===
The [[phonology]] of Old Kanembu is closely linked to the transcriptional possibilities offered by the [[Ajami alphabet]]. In particular, [[Tone (linguistics)|tonal]] distinctions are indicated through the contrast between [[Vowel length|short and long vowels]].<ref name=":6">{{Cite book |last=Bondarev |first=Dmitry |chapter=Old Kanembu and Kanuri in Arabic script: Phonology through the graphic system |chapter-url=https://www.academia.edu/26861840 |title=The Arabic Script in Africa |date=2014 |publisher=Brill |location=Leiden; Boston |isbn=9789004256804 |page=107}}</ref>

The phonological characteristics of Old Kanembu evolved over the four centuries documented by existing manuscripts. These phonological shifts are reflected in orthographic variations within Ajami writing, reflecting developments in vernacular languages. For instance, the letter ش (''shīn''), previously reserved for borrowings from Classical Arabic, was later repurposed to represent palatalized consonants in modern Kanuri, as in /shîm/ ‘eyes’.<ref name=":6" />

Moreover, several specific graphemes were employed to represent phonemes unique to spoken Kanuri.<ref name=":6" />

=== Grammar ===
Old Kanembu possesses an especially rich verbal system, characterized by fifteen categories of [[inflection]] and four categories of [[Derivation (linguistics)|derivation]].<ref name=":7">{{Cite journal |last=Bondarev |first=Dmitry |date=2020-12-30 |title=Absolute-relative tense in Old Kanembu: foregrounding by posterior taxis |url=https://iling-ran.ru/library/languageinafrica/1/LiA_4_15_Bondarev.pdf |journal=Language in Africa |volume=1 |issue=4 |pages=226–244 |doi=10.37892/2686-8946-2020-1-4-226-244}}</ref> A central feature of the language is its system of [[Focus (linguistics)|focus]], which can be either [[topic and comment|rhematic]] (absolute), emphasizing new information, or [[Theme (linguistics)|thematic]] (relative), referencing contextually known information. This focusing mechanism likely originates from [[Chadic languages]], notably [[Hausa language|Hausa]], which possesses analogous focus structures.<ref name=":7" />
